Read the spec from its compiled reference under .claude/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ./spec to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to .claude/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

The code is located in ./src.

The spec's Piton source is in ./spec, which `piton slice` reads. Don't change it, and don't read it directly to learn what the spec says: read the compiled reference, or what `piton slice` prints, instead.

Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.

content.text: Your results are in. Before I suggest a follow-up prompt, I'm reading the project's guide on how Suspense prompts work.

content.content:
# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user acts on; neither is ever sent by itself. A prompt card has buttons that send it to Code, Chain, or Spec, whichever mode it names, and one that puts it in the chat input to edit first.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.

content.text:
Run 1 fails badly. On your Radeon 890M at medium quality, the stage takes 4.0 ms per frame without trees and 42.0 ms with them, about 24 fps. That's 38 ms added against the spec's 1 ms budget.

| | No trees | With trees | Over budget by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average frame | 4.0 ms | 42.0 ms | +38 ms (budget is 1 ms) |
| 1% low | 10.4 ms | 98 ms | +88 ms (budget is 1 ms) |
| Worst frame | 13 ms | 418 ms | |
| Selection CPU time | | 1.34 ms | 13× (budget is 0.1 ms) |
| Load (cache hit) | | 478 ms | Passes (budget is 500 ms) |

**What it shows:**

1. **Almost all the cost is on the GPU.** Tree work on the CPU is about 3 ms a frame (1.3 ms selection plus a 1.5 ms batching job), so the remaining ~35 ms is GPU time. The reported tree GPU time (59 ms) is higher than the whole average frame, so treat it as a rough figure from a separate measured pass. Either way, the GPU is the bottleneck, which points at foliage overdraw and shadow casting.

2. **Static batching is mostly bypassed.** `active: 2434` means about 2,400 trees per frame go through the per-frame path: re-selected, written to the dynamic batches and uploaded to the GPU again. Only trees near a level threshold or mid-fade should be there. This is why selection is 13× over budget, and it adds an upload every frame. I haven't found the cause yet. Two possibilities: the 5 m rebuild job never finishes before the next one starts (its 1.5 ms is used up every frame), or the rule deciding which trees stay static rejects too many.

3. **The 300–400 ms spikes aren't CPU work.** Selection and the job stay around 1 ms and 1.5 ms in those frames, and no batch commit happens. That points to a GPU stall such as a shader compiling on first use or a large buffer upload. This is a guess, not yet confirmed.

**Next:** run #2 (`&treeprepass=1`) to see how much overdraw costs, and drive with #3 (`&treedebug=1`) to compare the main and shadow pass numbers. Then send this to Code mode. The spec already asks for these fixes, so only the code needs to change:

```suspense-prompt code
The tree benchmark on jackie at medium quality (Radeon 890M, 2117x1018) fails badly: trees add 38 ms to the average frame and 88 ms to the 1% low against a 1 ms budget, level selection takes 1.34 ms against 0.1 ms, and some frames spike to 300-400 ms while tree CPU work stays around 1-1.5 ms. The report shows 2,434 trees re-selected per frame, so almost every tree goes through the per-frame path instead of the static batches. Find out why so many trees are active and fix it, so only trees near a level threshold or in a fade are re-selected each frame. Find the cause of the 300-400 ms spikes and remove it. Then cut the GPU cost of the tree main and shadow passes toward the budget in .claude/reference/trees/Performance.md, using the mitigations it lists that are missing or turned off now: occlusion culling, the sprite depth prepass and the shadow cascade rules in .claude/reference/trees/Lod.md#shadows. Report the benchmark numbers before and after each fix.
```
